candidates.quote: Refrain tonight, / And that shall lend a kind of easiness / To the next abstinence, the next more easy; / For use almost can change the stamp of nature.
candidates.author: William Shakespeare
candidates.locator: Act 3, scene 4, Hamlet to Gertrude; Folger Shakespeare Library edition, 3.4.186 to 189 (Folger through line numbers 2622 to 2625, counting from 2437 at 3.4.1), partly a Second Quarto reading that the Folger prints; Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations enters these four lines on their own; the Folger line ends ‘nature,’ and the sentence runs on, so the closing full stop is the cut
candidates.whyThisMonth: Hamlet gives his mother the mechanics of habit in four lines: hold back once and the next time is easier, and the time after easier still, until practice has all but remade your nature.
candidates.speaker: Hamlet

candidates.quote: I know now, I understand at last, Constantine, that for us, whether we write or act, it is not the honour and glory of which I have dreamt that is important, it is the strength to endure.
candidates.author: Anton Chekhov
candidates.locator: Act IV, Nina to Treplieff (Constantine), her last long speech, the sentence before ‘One must know how to bear one’s cross, and one must have faith’; Plays by Anton Tchekoff, trans. Marian Fell (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1912); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 1754, which prints this version (Treplieff, Sea-Gull) without naming Fell on its title page
candidates.whyThisMonth: Nina has lost nearly everything and found the one thing this month is about: in writing or acting the glory is beside the point, and the craft is the strength to keep going.
candidates.speaker: Nina

candidates.quote: The last result of wisdom stamps it true: / He only earns his freedom and existence, / Who daily conquers them anew.
candidates.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
candidates.work: Faust: A Tragedy, The Second Part
candidates.locator: Act V, scene 6, Great Outer Court of the Palace, Faust’s last speech (German lines 11574 to 11576: Das ist der Weisheit letzter Schluß); trans. Bayard Taylor (Boston, 1871); text: Wikisource, Faust (trans. Bayard Taylor), Act V, VI, from the Houghton Mifflin reprint
candidates.whyThisMonth: Faust’s final conclusion, after a lifetime of chasing the one great moment, is that nothing is won once: freedom and life are earned again each day, which makes this morning the work.
candidates.speaker: Faust

candidates.quote: ’Tis early practice only makes the master.
candidates.author: Friedrich Schiller
candidates.locator: Act III, scene 1, Tell to Hedwig, as their boys play with a little crossbow (the German, a standing entry in Büchmann’s Geflügelte Worte: Früh übt sich, was ein Meister werden will); Wilhelm Tell, trans. Sir Theodore Martin (Bohn’s Standard Library); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 6788, which names Martin
candidates.whyThisMonth: A line that has been a German proverb for two centuries, said by a father watching his sons with a toy crossbow: mastery is nothing but practice begun early and kept up.
candidates.speaker: Wilhelm Tell
candidates.translator: Sir Theodore Martin, c. 1847 (Bohn’s Standard Library; the year is from secondary listings and is not confirmed against a title page)

candidates.quote: I believe that before all else I am a reasonable human being, just as you are—or, at all events, that I must try and become one.
candidates.author: Henrik Ibsen
candidates.locator: Act III, Nora to Helmer, in the final conversation, answering ‘Before all else, you are a wife and a mother’; A Doll’s House, trans. R. Farquharson Sharp (Everyman’s Library, J. M. Dent, 1910); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 2542, which names Sharp
candidates.whyThisMonth: The work of becoming, from the stage: Nora decides that being a person is a job she has to take up herself, and that thinking things through for herself is where it starts.
candidates.speaker: Nora

candidates.quote: But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach, though before that she was hard.
candidates.author: Hesiod
candidates.locator: lines 289 to 292, to his brother Perses; Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns and Homerica, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann, 1914), a prose translation, so it is given as prose; Bartlett’s enters the passage in another rendering; text: Project Gutenberg ebook 348
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest statement of the month’s theme, already a quotation by Plato’s day: the good is uphill and the sweat comes first, but the path that is rough at the start turns easy for whoever keeps climbing.

candidates.quote: Come now, have courage to be wise: begin: / You’re halfway over when you once plunge in: / He who puts off the time for mending, stands / A clodpoll by the stream with folded hands, / Waiting till all the water be gone past; / But it runs on, and will, while time shall last.
candidates.author: Horace
candidates.locator: Latin lines 40 to 43 (dimidium facti qui coepit habet; sapere aude; incipe); The Satires, Epistles, and Art of Poetry of Horace, trans. John Conington (Bell and Daldy, 1870); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 5419
candidates.whyThisMonth: The home of sapere aude, in Conington’s couplets: the person waiting for a better moment to begin is a bumpkin waiting for the river to finish running, so plunge in, because to have started is to be halfway over.

candidates.quote: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance, / As those move easiest who have learn’d to dance.
candidates.author: Alexander Pope
candidates.locator: Part II, lines 362 to 363; An Essay on Criticism (W. Lewis, 1711); spelling and pointing as in Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations and the Poetry Foundation text; Project Gutenberg ebook 7409, a school edition, prints ‘learned’ and drops the closing stop
candidates.whyThisMonth: A couplet by a poet who revised everything: the ease a reader admires is the residue of practice, as in dancing, which is good news for anyone who has to sit down and work at it today.

candidates.quote: Get leave to work / In this world,—’tis the best you get at all; / For God, in cursing, gives us better gifts / Than men in benediction.
candidates.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
candidates.locator: Third Book, lines 161 to 164 by my count in the 1857 text (quotation collections cite it as Bk. III, l. 164), in the passage beginning ‘Three years I lived and worked’; the quotation starts and stops mid-line; the fame signal is weak: the only reference entry I could open is Wikiquote’s Work page, and Bartlett’s ninth edition does not carry it; Aurora Leigh (Chapman and Hall, 1857); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 56621, a transcription of that edition
candidates.whyThisMonth: Aurora Leigh, three years into a garret and a vocation, decides that being allowed to work is the best thing this world hands out, and better than whatever the work is supposed to earn.
candidates.speaker: Aurora Leigh

candidates.quote: But he that dares not grasp the thorn / Should never crave the rose.
candidates.author: Anne Brontë
candidates.locator: lines 15 to 16, the close of the fourth stanza; The Complete Poems of Anne Brontë, ed. Clement Shorter (Hodder and Stoughton, 1920), as transcribed from the page scans at Wikisource; first printed in Fraser’s Magazine, December 1848, over the name Acton Bell
candidates.whyThisMonth: The youngest Brontë puts the terms of any discipline into two lines: the thorn comes with the rose, and wanting the one means being willing to take hold of the other.

candidates.quote: Climb Mount Fuji, / O snail, / but slowly, slowly.
candidates.author: Kobayashi Issa
candidates.work: ‘Climb Mount Fuji’ (katatsuburi / sorosoro nobore / fuji no yama)
candidates.locator: The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa, ed. and trans. Robert Hass (Ecco, 1994), Issa section; wording checked against the Lilliput Review listing of Hass’s Issa versions; R. H. Blyth’s older version (‘O snail / Climb Mount Fuji, / But slowly, slowly!’) is the one Salinger quotes in Franny and Zooey, and is not the wording given here
candidates.whyThisMonth: The patron poem of slow habit: the mountain is Fuji, the climber is a snail, and the only instruction is to keep going at a snail’s pace.

candidates.quote: I’ve learned to live simply, wisely, / To look at the sky and pray to God, / And to take long walks before evening / To wear out this useless anxiety.
candidates.author: Anna Akhmatova
candidates.work: ‘I’ve learned to live simply, wisely’ (Ya nauchilas prosto, mudro zhit, 1912), from Rosary (Chetki, 1914)
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4, the opening stanza; The Complete Poems of Anna Akhmatova, trans. Judith Hemschemeyer, ed. Roberta Reeder (Zephyr Press, 1990), Rosary section; wording checked against the Poetry Chaikhana reprint, which credits that book
candidates.whyThisMonth: A young poet lists the plain daily habits that steady her: look at the sky, pray, walk a long way before evening, and let the walking wear the worry out.

candidates.quote: Yes, there is goal and meaning in our path - / but it’s the way that is the labour’s worth.
candidates.author: Karin Boye
candidates.work: In Motion (I rörelse), from Härdarna (The Hearths, 1927)
candidates.locator: lines 3 to 4, the second couplet; Karin Boye: Complete Poems, trans. David McDuff (Bloodaxe Books, 1994), The Hearths; text as printed by the Karin Boye Society at karinboye.se (dikter-mcduff/in-motion), which sets a spaced hyphen after ‘path’ where the book may set a dash
candidates.whyThisMonth: Sweden’s most quoted couplet says the point of the road is the walking of it: there is a goal, but the day’s effort is what makes the journey worth making.

candidates.quote: Between my finger and my thumb / The squat pen rests. / I’ll dig with it.
candidates.author: Seamus Heaney
candidates.locator: the closing three lines (lines 29 to 31); Death of a Naturalist (Faber and Faber, 1966), the first poem in the book; text also at the Poetry Foundation
candidates.whyThisMonth: Having watched his father and grandfather dig, Heaney picks up the tool he has and calls writing what it is for anyone who does it daily: spadework.

candidates.quote: The pitcher cries for water to carry / and a person for work that is real.
candidates.author: Marge Piercy
candidates.locator: the closing two lines; To Be of Use (Doubleday, 1973); reprinted in Circles on the Water: Selected Poems of Marge Piercy (Alfred A. Knopf, 1982); text at the Poetry Foundation and at billmoyers.com (A Poet a Day)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last image of the poem that praises people who pull like water buffalo: a person wants real work the way a pitcher wants water, so the day’s task is a need met and not a burden.

candidates.quote: Live not for battles won. / Live not for the-end-of-the-song. / Live in the along.
candidates.author: Gwendolyn Brooks
candidates.work: Speech to the Young: Speech to the Progress-Toward (Among them Nora and Henry III)
candidates.locator: the closing three lines; Family Pictures (Broadside Press, 1970), the last poem in the book; reprinted in Blacks (Third World Press, 1991); text as printed by the Poetry Society of America (Poetry in Motion), which credits Blacks
candidates.whyThisMonth: Brooks tells the young not to live for the victory or the finished song but in the along, which is where every practice actually happens, this morning’s included.
